title: MDM Speaks with Our Founder: How a Second-Generation Distributor Built Avent
summary: Avent is the all-in-one AI platform for how distributors and suppliers actually do business.
body_text: We're excited to share that Modern Distribution Management (MDM), one of the most respected voices in the wholesale distribution industry, published a feature on Avent and our founder Abhay Kalra. The piece, written by MDM Senior Editor Vesna Brajkovic, explores how Abhay's experience growing up in his family's electrical and industrial distribution business in India shaped the vision behind Avent — and why he believes AI can unlock growth for distributors everywhere. From the Article "We had chances to grow, but the team didn't have time to go after new accounts; they were too busy processing what was already on their plate," Kalra told MDM. "And since everything depended on hiring, growth was always limited by how fast we could find and train good people." While studying electrical engineering and computer science at UC Berkeley, Kalra founded what he believes is the solution: Avent. What MDM Highlights The article covers Avent's three core automation capabilities: Quotes — finding correct product and pricing, generating quotes and preparing them for review Order Entry — matching purchase orders to earlier quotes, creating sales orders and inputting them into ERP systems Product Search — deciphering customer requests even when descriptions or part numbers don't match exactly "When a customer sends in an RFQ, the system finds the right pricing, generates a quote and sends it out," Kalra explains. "When a PO comes in, it's matched against the quote, and the sales order is created and entered into the ERP." Y Combinator Backing The article also notes Avent's acceptance into Y Combinator — the same accelerator behind Airbnb, Stripe and DoorDash — as a signal of investor confidence in the industrial distribution technology market. "A lot of very capable people try to build for this industry, but they underestimate how hard it is to get a clear answer by just asking, 'What's broken?'" Kalra said. "Most people will say, 'Nothing,' not because everything's perfect, but because they don't always know what's possible."

title: From Go code to container image with Depot API
summary: Build a specialized container building system using Depot's low-level Go SDK to transform tar archives into container images. This advanced walkthrough demonstrates the three-step build flow: registering builds, acquiring ephemeral BuildKit machines, and configuring custom build solutions.
body_text: In this post, we're going to create a more specialized container building system using the lower-level Depot API Go SDK. This is a more advanced use case that builds on our previous blog post . Here, we are going to create a tool that gets tar content and builds a container. How Depot's build flow works With the Depot API, there are three steps to build a container. Register a build with Depot. Acquire a Depot build machine. Configure, build, and push a container. Before you start Before you start, ensure you have a Depot project set up and an organization API token generated. Install the Go package To start, let's add these imports and run go mod tidy : import ( " context " " encoding/json " " log " " os " " time " " github.com/depot/depot-go/build " " github.com/depot/depot-go/machine " cliv1 " github.com/depot/depot-go/proto/depot/cli/v1 " " github.com/moby/buildkit/client " " github.com/moby/buildkit/session " " github.com/moby/buildkit/session/upload/uploadprovider " ) Register a build First, we request a new build with the Depot API. This request associates a build with a specific project's isolated cache. When registered, the Depot API will respond with the new build's ID and a one-time build token. We defer reporting the build result, buildErr, to the API. Any non-nil error is a build failure. token := os. Getenv ( "DEPOT_TOKEN" ) project := os. Getenv ( "DEPOT_PROJECT_ID" ) req := & cliv1 . CreateBuildRequest { ProjectId: project, } build, err := build. NewBuild (ctx, req, token) if err != nil { log. Fatal (err) } var buildErr error defer build. Finish (buildErr) Acquire a builder machine Next, we use the build ID and build token to request a new ephemeral builder machine. var buildkit * machine . Machine buildkit, buildErr = machine. Acquire (ctx, build.ID, build.Token, "arm64" ) if buildErr != nil { return } Since you're interacting directly with the underlying BuildKit in Depot, you must remember to release the machine when the build completes. By default, machines stay on for two minutes after a build to handle additional builds. defer buildkit. Release () Connect to BuildKit Once we have the BuildKit connection from the Acquire call, we connect to the machine’s BuildKit using mutual TLS. Once connected we can use all the power of BuildKit in Depot. var buildkitClient * client . Client buildkitClient, buildErr = buildkit. Connect (ctx) if buildErr != nil { return } Configure the build We create a BuildKit solver configuration. BuildKit conceptualizes builds as a graph of operations that are solved. In this case, we are going to configure the solver to receive a tar that contains the Dockerfile and all the needed content to run the build. /* * howdy.tar.gz is a compressed tar archive that contains the Dockerfile and * any other files needed to build the image. */ r, _ := os. Open ( "howdy.tar.gz" ) uploader := uploadprovider. New () // Special buildkit URL for HTTP over gRPC over gRPC. contextURL := uploader. Add (r) solverOptions := client . SolveOpt { Frontend: "dockerfile.v0" , FrontendAttrs: map [ string ] string { "platform" : "linux/arm64" , "context" : contextURL, // The tar file }, Session: [] session . Attachable { uploader, }, } We provide BuildKit with a session attachable uploader. We need to explain BuildKit's rather unique solutions to client/server communication. The reasons for this design choice are unclear. The "what" is a method for a server to request content from a client. An attachable is a BuildKit concept for a gRPC service hosted on the client on top of a bi-directional gRPC stream. This client-hosted service can be called by the server. In other words, the server tunnels gRPC requests back to the client. BuildKit's uploadprovider takes this tunneling approach further by layering HTTP/1.1 requests on top of the gRPC-over-gRPC connection. As you can imagine, this layering of networking can be brittle to network drops and thus build retries are not uncommon. ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │Buildkit Client │ │ Buildkit Server│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ ┌┴─┐ Layer 1: Client calls Server Session Service ┌──┤ │ │───(Bidirectional gRPC)────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌┴─┐ Layer 2: Server calls Client hosted Upload Service │ │ │ │ │ ◀────────────────────────────────────(Bi-Di gRPC tunneled over gRPC)──│ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Layer 3: Server asks for upload │ │ │ │ ┌┴─┐ ◀───────────────────────────────────(HTTP/1.1 over gRPC over gRPC)──│ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ▶ │ │ │ │ └┬─┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─▶ │ │ │ └┬─┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ◀ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ └─┬┘ └┬─┘ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ Nevertheless, we serve the tar file from the client to the BuildKit server over this protocol. Stream build output Next, we can run a goroutine that prints the output of each step of the build. buildStatusCh := make ( chan * client . SolveStatus , 10 ) go func () { enc := json. NewEncoder (os.Stdout) enc. SetIndent ( "" , " " ) for status := range buildStatusCh { _ = enc. Encode (status) } }() BuildKit will return status messages for each step of the build. Here, we're printing them as JSON to stdout. Build the container Lastly, we ask BuildKit to solve our request to build the container. The build will reuse cached steps stored in the project cache. _, buildErr = buildkitClient. Solve (ctx, nil , solverOptions, buildStatusCh) if buildErr != nil { return } With this example, you could build a service that receives a tar and creates an image. Conclusion With Depot's Go SDK, you can build sophisticated container building services without managing BuildKit infrastructure yourself. This approach gives you the performance benefits of Depot's optimized build machines—including native ARM64 support, persistent caches, and sub-second machine provisioning—while maintaining full control over the build process. The pattern we've explored here powers many production services that need programmatic container builds: CI/CD platforms, development environments, and SaaS applications that containerize user code. By leveraging Depot's API, you get enterprise-grade build performance without the operational overhead. Ready to get started? Generate an organization API token and explore our API documentation to begin building your own container services. FAQ What is Depot's Go SDK? Depot's Go SDK provides low-level access to BuildKit infrastructure for programmatic container builds. It allows you to build Docker images from your applications without managing BuildKit servers yourself. When should I use the API instead of the CLI? Use Depot's API when you need to build container images programmatically, such as in SaaS platforms that package user code or CI/CD systems that need custom build logic. The CLI is better for interactive development workflows. Do I need to manage BuildKit infrastructure? No, Depot handles all BuildKit infrastructure including machine provisioning, scaling, and maintenance. You get ephemeral build machines that spin up in seconds and automatically clean up after builds. How does caching work with the API? Each Depot project gets isolated cache storage that persists across builds. The BuildKit solver automatically reuses cached layers, dramatically speeding up subsequent builds with similar content. Related posts Now available: Depot API How to use BuildKit cache mounts in CI BuildKit in-depth: Docker's build engine explained Chris Goller Principal Software Engineer at Depot

title: Real-Time And Embeddable Analytics for Growing SaaS Teams: A 2025 Comparison Guide
summary: Compare the top real-time and embedded BI tools for SaaS teams. Discover how self-service analytics helps marketing, sales, and product teams move faster in…
body_text: Remember when getting a simple report meant filing a ticket with your data team and waiting two weeks? Those days are over. While your competitors are still wrestling with spreadsheets and begging their data team for basic charts, smart companies are already making decisions with live data that updates faster than their coffee gets cold. SaaS business intelligence tools have completely flipped the script on how mid-market companies work with data. No more waiting around for IT to set up servers or spending months just to see your basic metrics. Product managers can now spot user trends in real-time. Sales ops can catch pipeline issues before they tank the quarter. Marketing teams can actually optimize campaigns while they’re running, not three weeks later. This isn’t just about having shinier dashboards. It’s about removing all the annoying friction between having a question and getting an answer. And honestly, it’s about time. Understanding SaaS BI Tools SaaS business intelligence tools are basically analytics platforms that live in the cloud and don’t make you want to pull your hair out. Unlike those old-school BI systems that needed their own server room and a PhD to operate, these tools just connect to your existing apps and start showing you useful stuff through your browser. Here’s what makes them different: they actually talk to each other. Your CRM data plays nice with your marketing tools, which connects to your product analytics, which links to your financial software. No more hunting through five different systems to understand what’s happening in your business. The real game-changer is that everything updates live. When someone signs up for your product, that data shows up in your dashboard immediately. When a marketing campaign goes live, you see the results as they happen. It’s like having a pulse on your business instead of getting an autopsy report three days later. And here’s the best part: regular people can actually use these things. Your product manager doesn’t need to learn SQL. Your sales director doesn’t need to submit a ticket every time they want to see conversion rates by source. Everyone can dig into the data themselves, which means decisions happen way faster. The fancy term for this is “self-service analytics,” but really it just means your tools finally work the way you think they should. Definition of SaaS BI Tools Let’s cut through the buzzwords. SaaS BI tools are analytics platforms that run entirely online, which means you don’t need to buy servers, hire database administrators, or wait months for someone to set everything up. The “cloud-native” part means everything runs in the vendor’s data centers. You just log in through your browser, whether you’re at the office, working from your kitchen table, or traveling. No installations, no updates, no IT headaches. Most of these platforms can connect to your business apps within hours, not months. We’re talking about getting your first useful dashboard up and running faster than it takes to onboard a new employee. Updates happen automatically too. Remember how your old BI system ran the same version for years while you watched competitors get cool new features? That doesn’t happen anymore. These platforms keep getting better without you having to do anything. The pricing makes sense too. Instead of paying huge upfront costs that scared off smaller companies, you typically pay per user or based on how much data you’re working with. It’s like the difference between buying a house and renting an apartment. Companies using these tools report growing 10-30% faster than their competitors who are still stuck with manual reporting. That’s not magic, it’s just what happens when you can actually respond to what your data is telling you. How SaaS BI Tools Differ from Traditional BI Tools The difference between new SaaS BI tools and traditional ones isn’t subtle. It’s like comparing a smartphone to one of those old Nokia bricks. Traditional BI projects were basically software archaeology. Six to eighteen months of planning, installation, configuration, and training just to get basic reports. SaaS tools get you up and running with real dashboards in days. With old systems, you needed a whole IT department just to keep the lights on. Database administrators, server maintenance, software updates, the works. SaaS tools need an internet connection and someone who can click “connect” when setting up integrations. Updates used to be a nightmare. Remember planning upgrade cycles and hoping nothing broke? Now everything just gets better automatically while you sleep. Scaling traditional systems meant buying more hardware, negotiating new licenses, and crossing your fingers that performance wouldn’t tank. With SaaS tools, you usually just adjust your subscription and boom, you can handle more users or data. But here’s the biggest difference: data freshness. Old systems relied on overnight batch jobs that made your reports feel like reading yesterday’s newspaper. Modern SaaS tools show you what’s happening right now, not what happened yesterday after the nightly data processing finally finished. Importance of Real-Time Data in SaaS BI Real-time data changes everything about how you run your business. Instead of finding out about problems in next week’s report, you see them happening and can actually do something about it. When your dashboards update continuously, you stop being reactive and start being responsive. Product launches can be tweaked based on early user behavior. Marketing campaigns get optimized while they’re actually running. Customer service issues get resolved before they turn into angry Twitter threads. Think about competitive advantage this way: while your competitors are analyzing last week’s trends in their monthly review meeting, you’re already responding to patterns that are happening today. That head start compounds over time. Teams also work more efficiently when they don’t have to wait around for data. Questions get answered immediately instead of going into some backlog. Problems get spotted and fixed during business hours instead of being discovered in scheduled reports. Plus, you can set up smart alerts that notify the right people when important metrics cross certain thresholds. No more nasty surprises during board meetings. Enhancing Strategic Decision-Making Real-time dashboards completely change how leadership teams make big decisions. Instead of relying on month-old data in board presentations, executives can see what’s actually happening right now. When you’re planning different strategic options, you can model scenarios using current market conditions instead of making assumptions based on old data. This makes your forecasts way more accurate and gives everyone more confidence in major decisions. All departments start working from the same playbook when everyone has access to the same live data. Marketing knows what sales is seeing, product understands what customer success is dealing with, and operations can coordinate with everyone else without waiting for formal reporting cycles. Investment decisions get better too. Whether you’re evaluating which marketing channels actually work, which product features people actually use, or which operational improvements are worth the effort, real-time data gives you the current context you need. Risk management becomes proactive instead of reactive. Instead of discovering problems in monthly reports, you spot potential issues immediately and can actually prevent them from becoming bigger problems. Improving Operational Efficiency Real-time operational data eliminates most of those annoying delays that slow everything down. Teams can identify and fix issues during normal business hours instead of discovering them in reports three days later. Customer success teams can spot usage pattern changes immediately instead of waiting for quarterly business reviews. Sales managers can address pipeline issues while deals are still salvageable. Product teams can respond to user feedback while users are still engaged. Resource allocation becomes way more responsive. Support teams can adjust staffing based on actual ticket volume trends. Marketing teams can shift budget to channels that are actually working. Operations teams can optimize inventory based on real demand instead of last month’s guesses. Process improvements happen faster too. A/B tests show results immediately. Process changes show impact right away. Training effectiveness can be measured in real-time instead of waiting for quarterly reviews. The best part is that all this happens within your existing workflows. Teams keep using the tools they already know, they just get better information to make better decisions. The Role of Instantaneous Metrics Instant metrics turn your dashboard from a rearview mirror into a live speedometer. When key performance indicators update continuously, you can treat data as a feedback system instead of a historical record. Customer behavior insights appear immediately, so product and marketing teams can understand how users respond to changes as they happen. Feature releases get optimized based on immediate usage patterns. Onboarding flows get adjusted based on real-time completion rates. Sales pipeline visibility means revenue teams can address issues before they kill the quarter. Deal progression, conversion rates, and pipeline velocity metrics work like early warning systems that trigger the right interventions at the right time. Marketing campaign performance can be optimized while campaigns are still live instead of doing post-mortems after all the budget is spent. Money shifts to high-performing channels immediately. Creative gets adjusted based on early response data. Audience targeting gets refined continuously. Financial performance tracking gives leadership teams current visibility into burn rates, customer acquisition costs, and revenue without waiting for month-end close. This means faster course corrections and more accurate forecasting. When you combine instant metrics with smart alerts, you get management systems that prevent problems instead of just identifying them after they’ve already caused damage. Benefits of Embedded BI in SaaS Embedded business intelligence is like having analytics superpowers built right into the tools you already use every day. Instead of switching between your CRM and some separate analytics platform, the insights just show up where you need them. Customer success teams see usage analytics right in their CRM. Product managers get feature adoption data in their project management tools. Sales teams view pipeline insights within their sales platforms. No more toggling between tabs or losing your train of thought. User adoption goes through the roof when analytics show up in familiar places. Teams don’t need training on new platforms or complicated processes. The learning curve basically disappears when BI capabilities just appear seamlessly in tools people already know. Decisions happen faster when relevant data appears automatically in context. Account managers see customer health scores right in contact records. Support teams see ticket trends in their help desk interface. Finance teams see spending analytics in their expense management tools. You can also create role-specific dashboards that actually match what people need for their jobs instead of generic analytics that try to serve everyone and end up helping no one. Seamless Integration with Existing Systems Modern SaaS BI tools are really good at playing nice with whatever tech stack you’ve already built. These integrations eliminate data silos by pulling information from multiple sources into unified views that actually make sense. Most common business apps connect through pre-built integrations. Your CRM, marketing automation platform, customer support tools, financial software, and product analytics all link up through standard connections that typically just need basic permission setup. For custom applications or specialized industry software, robust APIs let your technical team connect proprietary systems without too much hassle. The data stays in sync without slowing down your operational applications. Most platforms use smart sync processes that capture changes without affecting day-to-day business operations. Single sign-on means your team doesn’t have to manage yet another set of passwords. Everyone can access analytics using their existing corporate credentials. Real-time sync ensures your insights reflect what’s actually happening in your business right now, not some outdated snapshot from yesterday’s batch job. Customizable Dashboards for Tailored Insights Customizable dashboards solve that annoying “one size fits nobody” problem. Different people need different information, presented in ways that actually match how they make decisions. Sales reps focus on their personal pipeline and quota progress. Sales managers need to see team performance and forecast accuracy. Marketing managers track campaign performance while executives want to monitor overall customer acquisition efficiency. Everyone gets what they need without wading through irrelevant metrics. Industry-specific templates give you a head start instead of building everything from scratch. SaaS companies can start with templates for monthly recurring revenue, churn analysis, and customer lifetime value, then customize from there. Some people prefer detailed tables while others work better with high-level charts. Good BI platforms support different visualization styles for the same data, so everyone can process information in their preferred format. Interactive features let users explore data dynamically instead of being stuck with static views. Drill-down functionality, filtering options, and flexible time ranges enable self-service analysis that adapts to changing questions. White-label options keep everything on-brand when BI capabilities are embedded in customer-facing applications or shared with external stakeholders. Self-Service Capabilities for Users Self-service analytics eliminate those annoying bottlenecks that slow everything down. When team members can answer their own questions immediately, both productivity and data literacy improve across the organization. Drag-and-drop report building lets non-technical users create custom analysis without writing code or submitting IT tickets. Business questions get explored immediately instead of joining some development queue that might take weeks to address. Natural language querying removes the barrier of learning query languages or understanding database structures. Questions like “show me customer churn by signup month” automatically generate the right visualizations without requiring any technical knowledge. Automated insights proactively surface interesting patterns and anomalies that might otherwise go unnoticed. Machine learning algorithms identify trending metrics, unusual performance patterns, and correlation insights that inform strategic decisions. Sharing features let teams distribute insights effectively without creating additional reporting overhead. Analysis can be shared through links, embedded in presentations, or distributed through scheduled emails that update automatically. When users find something interesting in a dashboard, they can drill down into underlying data to understand what’s really happening without needing specialized analytical skills. Key Features of Real-Time SaaS BI Tools Real-time SaaS BI tools share several core capabilities that make them actually useful for modern business operations. These features work together to create analytics experiences that match how fast business actually moves. Live data connections keep everything current instead of relying on those old overnight batch updates. When sales opportunities update in your CRM, changes appear immediately in sales dashboards. When customers upgrade subscriptions, revenue metrics reflect the change instantly. Interactive visualization engines respond immediately to user inputs like filtering, drilling down, or changing time ranges. You can follow your natural thought process while exploring data instead of having to plan out query sequences in advance. Automated alerting systems monitor key metrics continuously and ping the right people when important thresholds get crossed. Critical changes get immediate attention instead of being buried in routine dashboard reviews. Collaborative sharing lets teams distribute insights effectively while keeping data secure and maintaining appropriate access controls. You can share analysis with the right stakeholders without compromising sensitive information. Mobile accessibility means team members can check critical business metrics regardless of location or device. This flexibility supports remote work and enables decision-making outside traditional office environments. Real-Time Data Updates Real-time data capabilities transform business intelligence from a periodic reporting chore into a continuous monitoring and decision-making system. This shift enables more responsive management and faster identification of both opportunities and problems. Streaming data processing handles high-volume, fast-moving data sources that traditional systems choke on. Customer interaction data, application usage metrics, and transaction information get processed and analyzed as events occur instead of hours or days later. Change data capture identifies and processes only the records that actually changed instead of reprocessing entire datasets every time. This efficiency enables real-time updates while minimizing system resource consumption and keeping operational applications running smoothly. Event-driven updates trigger immediate dashboard refreshes when significant business events occur. Product releases, marketing campaign launches, and customer onboarding milestones automatically update relevant analytics without manual intervention. Conflict resolution handles it when multiple sources provide overlapping or contradictory information. Modern platforms sort out timing differences and conflicting updates intelligently to maintain analytical accuracy. Performance optimization keeps dashboards loading quickly even when processing large volumes of real-time data. Advanced caching, query optimization, and infrastructure scaling ensure responsive user experiences regardless of underlying data complexity. Robust Analytics and Visualization Solutions Advanced analytical capabilities separate professional BI platforms from basic charting tools. These features enable sophisticated analysis that scales from simple trend monitoring to complex statistical modeling. AI-powered insights automatically identify patterns and anomalies that might slip past manual analysis. Machine learning algorithms spot seasonal trends, detect unusual customer behavior, and highlight metrics that deviate from expected ranges. Predictive analytics turns past data into future insights. Forecasting models predict customer churn, estimate revenue growth, and identify future resource requirements based on current trends and business patterns. Statistical analysis tools provide confidence intervals, correlation analysis, and significance testing without requiring specialized statistical software. Business users can validate hypotheses and quantify relationships between different business metrics. Advanced visualization options support complex data relationships through heat maps, network diagrams, and multidimensional analysis. These help with pattern recognition that simple charts just can’t provide. Custom calculation engines let users create business-specific metrics that combine data from multiple sources. Complex formulas for customer lifetime value, marketing attribution, and operational efficiency can be implemented without any coding. Scalability and Performance Optimization Scalability ensures BI platforms keep delivering snappy performance as organizations grow and data volumes increase. This prevents analytics from becoming bottlenecks that slow down business operations. Elastic infrastructure automatically adjusts computing resources based on usage demand instead of requiring manual capacity planning. Peak usage periods don’t slow things down, and quiet times don’t waste infrastructure costs. Query optimization improves response times through intelligent caching, parallel processing, and efficient data retrieval. Complex analysis completes quickly even when working with large datasets or multiple data sources. User concurrency support maintains performance when multiple team members access analytics simultaneously. Shared resources get managed efficiently to prevent individual queries from affecting overall system responsiveness. Data compression and indexing minimize storage requirements and speed up query performance. These optimizations reduce infrastructure costs while improving user experience across all analytical functions. Geographic distribution ensures consistent performance for distributed teams by keeping data copies in multiple regions. Remote team members get the same snappy performance as people at headquarters. Popular Real-Time SaaS BI Tools For 2025 The real-time SaaS BI market includes both big enterprise vendors and scrappy new platforms built specifically for modern business needs. Each tool has different strengths that appeal to various organizational requirements and technical comfort levels. Market leaders like Tableau and Power BI offer comprehensive feature sets with tons of integrations and large user communities. These platforms work well in environments that need advanced analytical capabilities and can handle longer implementation timelines. Newer platforms focus on specific use cases or offer streamlined user experiences that cut through complexity and get you up and running fast. These tools often have more intuitive interfaces and quicker deployment than traditional enterprise solutions. Industry-specific solutions optimize for particular business models or vertical market requirements. SaaS companies, e-commerce businesses, and professional services can find platforms tailored to their specific needs and common metrics. Integration specialists excel at connecting diverse tech stacks and handling complex data source requirements. These platforms work well for organizations with substantial existing system investments that need comprehensive connectivity. Choosing between platforms usually depends on technical requirements, user comfort levels, budget constraints, and specific feature priorities rather than any single solution being objectively better. Basedash AI-Native BI for SaaS Insights Basedash is an AI-native business intelligence platform and focuses specifically on modern SaaS companies that need immediate insights without complexity. The platform emphasizes natural language querying and automated data warehouse setup to eliminate traditional BI implementation headaches. You can generate visualizations by asking questions in plain English instead of learning query syntax or database structures. Questions like “show me monthly recurring revenue by customer segment” automatically create the right charts without any technical knowledge required. The automated data pipeline setup connects to over 750 data sources and creates optimized data warehouses without manual configuration. This eliminates the weeks or months typically required for traditional BI implementations. Flat-rate pricing removes per-seat limitations that can restrict analytics access in growing organizations. Teams can give BI capabilities to entire organizations without worrying about escalating license costs as headcount increases. Real-time dashboard updates ensure insights reflect current business conditions instead of outdated snapshots. Customer behavior changes, revenue updates, and operational metrics appear immediately rather than after scheduled data processing cycles. Collaborative sharing features let teams distribute insights effectively while maintaining appropriate access controls. Analysis can be embedded in presentations, shared through links, or distributed via automated reports that update continuously. You can try Basedash for free now to learn how easy it is to get charts from natural language. Embeddable: Developer’s Choice for Embedded Analytics Embeddable is a unique and powerful option that is quickly gaining market share with SaaS tools in the embedded analytics space. Their headless embedded analytics approach provides a highly scalable, configurable and extensible platform that enables product and engineering teams to deliver fast, fully-custom dashboards inside their apps, with complete control over performance, UX, and developer workflow. Dashboards and reports blend seamlessly into your application’s UI/UX thanks to code-level control over every pixel; and rendering via secure and lightweight React/Vue embeds or via web components (no iframes). Your customers will experience excellent loading performance at scale, supported by a two-layer configurable cache and high-performance data service that enable you to deliver real-time, ‘near realtime’ or whatever data latency and data freshness balance meets your needs. It has the built-in features you need for customer-facing analytics, such as export options, drills, localization, and a powerful self-serve option that lets teams deliver more value to customers faster. From there, you have full control to theme, extend, or even import charts from any React library to make it fully unique. Embeddable is built for software engineers. Intuitive SDKs, APIs, versioning and CI/CD integrations that fit naturally into modern stacks and development workflows. Developers can extend, theme, and customize every chart in code (or drop in their own charting libraries) without limitations. Connections are available for all major databases, it supports single- and multi-tenant architectures, and it embeds into any frontend. It adapts to your infrastructure, deployment, and monitoring strategies, scaling securely from QA to staging to production. Tableau Advanced Data Visualization Platform Tableau is one of the most advanced visualization platforms. It offers strong analysis tools that attract data-focused companies. These companies are willing to invest in full BI setups. The advanced visualization engine supports complex chart types, interactive dashboards, and sophisticated analytical functions that enable deep data exploration. Users can create publication-quality visualizations that communicate insights effectively to different audiences. Extensive connector library integrates with hundreds of data sources through pre-built connections and custom API integrations. This flexibility accommodates complex tech stacks and specialized industry applications. Desktop and server deployment options provide flexibility for organizations with specific security or performance requirements. On-premise installations can handle sensitive data requirements that cloud-only solutions can’t address. The large user community provides extensive resources for learning, troubleshooting, and best practice sharing. Training materials, user forums, and third-party consulting services support successful implementations across different organizational contexts. AI-powered insights through Einstein Discovery automatically identify patterns and suggest relevant analysis paths. These capabilities help users discover insights that might otherwise require specialized statistical expertise. Microsoft Power BI Integration with Microsoft Ecosystem Microsoft Power BI leverages tight integration with the Microsoft ecosystem to provide comprehensive BI capabilities that work seamlessly with familiar productivity tools and enterprise systems. Office 365 integration enables natural workflows between Excel, SharePoint, Teams, and analytics functions. Business users can move between familiar Microsoft tools and advanced BI capabilities without jarring context switches. Azure cloud services provide scalable infrastructure and advanced analytical capabilities including machine learning and AI services. Companies can do complex analyses. They do not have to handle the technical details behind them. Cost-effective pricing makes enterprise-grade BI capabilities accessible to mid-market organizations, especially those already invested in Microsoft licensing. Per-user costs compare favorably to competing enterprise platforms. Mobile applications provide full-featured access to dashboards and reports across different device types. Remote team members can access critical business metrics with the same functionality available on desktop computers. Self-service capabilities allow business users to create and modify reports without IT involvement. Drag-and-drop interfaces and pre-built templates speed up dashboard creation and reduce technical barriers to adoption. How Qlik Sense Enables Associative Data Analytics Qlik Sense differentiates itself through associative analytics that reveal data relationships and patterns that traditional query-based systems might miss. This approach enables more exploratory and intuitive data analysis experiences. The associative engine allows users to explore data relationships dynamically instead of being constrained by pre-defined queries or data models. This flexibility supports investigative analysis that follows natural thought processes and curiosity. Self-service analytics empower business users to create and modify analyses without technical assistance. Drag-and-drop interfaces and intelligent suggestions guide users through complex analytical processes. Responsive design adapts dashboards automatically to different screen sizes and device types. Users get consistent functionality whether accessing analytics through desktop computers, tablets, or smartphones. In-memory processing delivers fast performance even when working with large datasets or complex calculations. Interactive exploration stays responsive regardless of underlying data complexity or query sophistication. Collaborative features enable teams to share insights, build on each other’s analysis, and coordinate decision-making processes effectively. Comments, annotations, and shared workspaces support team-based analytical workflows. Choosing the Right SaaS BI Tool Picking the right SaaS BI platform requires honest evaluation of what your organization actually needs, what technical constraints you’re working with, and what you’re trying to achieve strategically. The right choice balances current needs with future growth plans while considering user capabilities and budget reality. How technical your team is significantly influences platform selection. Organizations with data-savvy teams can take advantage of advanced platforms with comprehensive feature sets, while companies prioritizing ease-of-use might prefer streamlined solutions with intuitive interfaces. Data complexity requirements determine what kind of integration capabilities and analytical depth you actually need. Simple reporting needs can be met by basic platforms, while complex multi-source analysis requires more sophisticated data processing and visualization capabilities. Budget considerations include both upfront costs and ongoing expenses as usage scales. Per-user pricing works well for small teams but can get expensive as organizations grow, while flat-rate options provide predictable costs but might include features you’ll never use. How urgently you need this varies based on business needs and available technical resources. Some platforms deliver immediate value through rapid deployment, while others require longer setup periods but provide more comprehensive capabilities. Future growth needs should influence decisions even when current requirements are modest. Platform selection affects long-term analytical capabilities and switching costs, so thinking about growth accommodation is important. Factors to Consider for Scalability Scalability evaluation ensures BI platforms can handle organizational growth without requiring disruptive migrations or performance compromises. Several key factors determine how well different solutions handle increasing demands. Data volume handling becomes critical as businesses generate more operational data. Platforms should maintain snappy performance as dataset sizes grow from megabytes to gigabytes or terabytes without requiring infrastructure changes. User concurrency support determines how many team members can access analytics simultaneously without affecting system performance. Growing organizations need platforms that handle increased usage gracefully rather than slowing down user experience. Integration scalability accommodates additional data sources and business applications as tech stacks expand. Platforms should connect new systems efficiently without requiring architectural changes or custom development work. Geographic distribution capabilities support remote teams and international expansion. Global organizations need BI platforms that maintain consistent performance across different regions and time zones. Feature scalability lets companies add advanced tools. These include predictive analytics, machine learning, or special industry modules as their analysis grows. Platform selection should anticipate future requirements rather than just addressing current needs. Ensuring Performance Optimization Performance optimization keeps users productive and happy as BI implementations mature and expand. Several technical factors determine how well platforms handle increasing complexity and usage demands. Query response times directly affect user experience and adoption rates. Platforms should deliver consistently fast results even when processing complex analyses or large datasets. Slow performance discourages usage and reduces analytical effectiveness. Caching strategies improve responsiveness by storing frequently accessed data and calculations in high-speed storage. Good caching reduces server load while ensuring users get immediate responses to common queries. Data compression techniques minimize storage requirements and network transfer times without compromising analytical accuracy. Efficient compression reduces infrastructure costs while improving overall system performance. Parallel processing uses modern computer designs. It handles many requests at the same time efficiently. This prevents individual users or complex queries from affecting overall system responsiveness. Automated optimization adjusts system performance based on usage patterns and data characteristics without requiring manual intervention. Self-tuning systems maintain optimal performance as business requirements evolve and data volumes increase. Evaluating Cost-Effectiveness of BI Platforms Cost-effectiveness evaluation considers both direct expenses and indirect value creation to determine overall return on investment from BI platform implementations. Several factors influence long-term financial impact beyond just initial licensing costs. Licensing model flexibility affects total costs as organizations grow and usage patterns change. Per-user models work well for small teams but can get expensive with growth, while flat-rate options provide cost predictability but might include unused features. Implementation cost requirements include setup, training, integration, and customization expenses beyond platform licensing. Some solutions require extensive professional services while others enable self-service deployment that minimizes consulting costs. Operational efficiency gains create value through faster decision-making, reduced manual reporting overhead, and improved analytical accuracy. These benefits often justify platform costs through productivity improvements and better business outcomes. Maintenance and support costs vary significantly between platforms and deployment models. Cloud solutions typically include maintenance and updates in subscription costs, while on-premise implementations require dedicated IT resources. Opportunity cost considerations evaluate potential revenue loss from delayed insights or missed opportunities. More expensive platforms might provide better ROI if they enable faster response to market changes or competitive threats. Maximizing the Use of BI Tools in SaaS Getting maximum value from BI implementation goes way beyond just picking the right platform. Organizations that achieve the best results treat BI as a strategic capability that requires ongoing attention rather than just a reporting tool they set up once. Data governance frameworks ensure accuracy, consistency, and security across all analytical processes. Good governance prevents conflicting metrics, maintains data quality, and establishes appropriate access controls that balance transparency with security requirements. User training and adoption programs accelerate organizational learning and ensure teams can actually use platform capabilities effectively. Training should address both technical skills and analytical thinking, not just software button-clicking. Cross-functional collaboration maximizes insight value by ensuring different departments can share analysis and coordinate decision-making processes. Siloed analytics limit organizational learning and miss opportunities for strategic alignment. Continuous improvement processes adapt BI capabilities to changing business needs and emerging opportunities. Regular platform evaluation, user feedback collection, and capability enhancement ensure BI investments keep delivering value as organizations evolve. Integration optimization maintains performance and reliability as data sources and user requirements change. Ongoing integration management prevents technical debt that can compromise system effectiveness over time. Effective Data Integration Techniques Successful data integration makes BI platforms effective. It ensures information is accurate, timely, and complete. Different integration methods meet various company needs and technical limits. API-first integration strategies provide flexible, maintainable connections that adapt to changing business systems and requirements. Modern APIs enable real-time data synchronization without affecting operational system performance or creating complex dependencies. ETL process optimization ensures data transformations maintain accuracy while minimizing processing time and resource consumption. Efficient ETL processes enable real-time analytics without overwhelming source systems or creating performance bottlenecks. Data quality monitoring identifies and resolves accuracy issues before they affect analytical outputs. Automated quality checks, exception reporting, and data validation rules prevent unreliable insights that can undermine decision-making confidence. Master data management maintains consistency across multiple systems and prevents conflicting information from undermining analytical accuracy. Centralized data definitions ensure metrics mean the same thing across different departments and applications. Change management processes accommodate updates to source systems, business processes, and reporting requirements without disrupting ongoing analytical operations. Good change management prevents integration failures that can interrupt business intelligence availability. Leveraging Customization for Business Needs Customization lets BI platforms fit company needs and user choices. It stops businesses from changing their processes to fit generic software. Smart customization improves adoption and analytical effectiveness. Role-based dashboard design ensures each team member sees information relevant to their specific responsibilities and decision-making authority. Customized views improve focus and reduce information overload that can hurt analytical effectiveness. Industry-specific metric implementations accommodate specialized business models and performance indicators that generic platforms might not support naturally. Custom calculations enable proper measurement of unique business processes and competitive factors. Branding and visual consistency maintain organizational identity when BI capabilities are embedded in customer-facing applications or shared with external stakeholders. White-label options ensure analytical presentations align with overall brand experience. Workflow integration embeds analytical capabilities within existing business processes instead of requiring separate tools or additional steps. Integrated workflows improve adoption by eliminating context switching and reducing administrative overhead. Alert and notification customization ensures relevant team members get appropriate information at optimal times without creating notification fatigue. Personalized alerts help people respond faster. They also reduce too much information. Continuous Monitoring and Adapting BI Practices Continuous improvement ensures BI implementations stay effective as business requirements evolve and organizational capabilities mature. Regular evaluation and optimization prevent analytical capabilities from becoming outdated or misaligned with strategic objectives. Usage analytics identify which features provide value and which elements go unused, enabling optimization that focuses resources on high-impact capabilities. Usage patterns reveal opportunities for training, customization, or platform enhancement. Performance monitoring checks system speed, accuracy, and reliability. It stops problems that hurt user experience and analysis quality. Proactive monitoring enables issue resolution before problems impact business operations. User feedback collection captures insights about functionality gaps, usability issues, and feature requests that guide platform evolution. Regular feedback ensures BI capabilities continue meeting changing organizational needs and user expectations. Business requirement evolution necessitates periodic review of metrics, dashboards, and analytical processes to ensure alignment with current strategic priorities. Business changes should trigger corresponding BI capability updates. Technology landscape changes require integration updates, security enhancements, and functionality expansion to maintain platform effectiveness. Ongoing technology management ensures BI investments keep delivering value as business systems evolve. The Future of SaaS BI Tools The evolution of SaaS business intelligence keeps accelerating through advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and natural language processing. These tech improvements promise to make analytics even more accessible and valuable for mid-market organizations. Predictive capabilities will become standard features instead of expensive premium options, enabling organizations to forecast trends and identify opportunities with greater accuracy and less technical complexity. Machine learning models will provide insights that anticipate business changes instead of just reporting what already happened. Natural language interfaces will eliminate the remaining barriers between business questions and data answers. Conversational analytics will let team members explore data through normal speech patterns instead of learning specialized query languages or dashboard navigation. Automated insight generation will proactively surface important patterns and anomalies instead of waiting for users to discover them manually. AI-powered analysis will identify trends, correlations, and outliers that human analysis might miss while providing context that explains their business significance. Real-time collaboration features will enable distributed teams to work together on analysis projects seamlessly. Shared analytical workspaces will combine individual expertise with collective intelligence to improve decision-making quality and speed. The convergence of these capabilities will transform business intelligence from a specialized technical function into a natural extension of business communication and decision-making processes. Impact of SaaS BI Tools on Mid-Market Companies SaaS business intelligence tools have completely changed how mid-market companies access and use data for decision-making. The shift from complex, expensive enterprise systems to accessible, cloud-native platforms puts analytics capabilities that used to be available only to huge organizations within reach of normal businesses. Real-time data access, intuitive interfaces, and embedded analytical capabilities eliminate most of the barriers that historically prevented organizations from becoming truly data-driven. Teams can now answer business questions immediately instead of waiting for IT support or scheduled reporting cycles. The competitive advantage of faster, better-informed decision-making keeps growing as markets become more dynamic and customer expectations evolve more rapidly. Organizations that figure out modern BI capabilities position themselves to respond effectively to opportunities and challenges that competitors discover too late. Success requires more than just picking the right platform. Organizations need to invest in data governance, user training, and continuous optimization to get maximum value from their BI investment. But companies that commit to this transformation typically see significant performance improvements and sustained competitive advantages. The future promises even greater accessibility and sophistication as AI capabilities keep advancing. Organizations that build strong BI foundations now will be positioned to take advantage of emerging capabilities that further accelerate business performance and strategic effectiveness. Choose platforms that match your current needs while providing room for growth. Focus on solutions that integrate seamlessly with existing workflows instead of requiring disruptive process changes. Most importantly, treat BI implementation as an organizational capability that requires ongoing attention and optimization rather than a one-time technology purchase. The transformation to data-driven decision-making isn’t just about better tools. It’s about creating organizational cultures that value evidence over opinion, speed over perfection, and continuous learning over static processes. SaaS BI tools provide the foundation for this transformation, but sustained success depends on commitment to analytical thinking and data-informed action across all levels of the organization.

title: Teknova Reports Second Quarter 2025 Financial Results
summary: Second quarter 2025 total revenue was $10.3 million, up 7% from prior year Achieves four consecutive quarters of year-over-year revenue growth Company reaffirms 2025 revenue guidance of $39-42 million HOLLISTER, Calif., Aug. 07, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Alpha Teknova, Inc.
body_text: < Back Teknova Reports Second Quarter 2025 Financial Results August 7, 2025 at 4:01 PM EDT PDF Version Second quarter 2025 total revenue was $10.3 million, up 7% from prior year Achieves four consecutive quarters of year-over-year revenue growth Company reaffirms 2025 revenue guidance of $39-42 million HOLLISTER, Calif., Aug. 07, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Alpha Teknova, Inc. (“Teknova” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: TKNO), a leading producer of critical reagents for the discovery, development, and commercialization of novel therapies, vaccines, and molecular diagnostics, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2025. “Despite continued uncertainty in the macroenvironment, we delivered another strong quarter of results, with improvements in both the top and bottom lines,” said Stephen Gunstream, President and Chief Executive Officer at Teknova. “We continue to believe that the investments we’ve made in our operational and commercial infrastructure, combined with our diverse product portfolio and customer base, position Teknova for sustainable, above-market growth over the long-term.” Matt Lowell, Teknova’s Chief Financial Officer, added, “Compared to 2024, we delivered 7% revenue growth in the second quarter 2025 along with significant improvements in adjusted EBITDA and free cash outflow. We believe the Company is well positioned to maintain its momentum. We therefore reiterate our 2025 revenue guidance of $39-42 million and continue to anticipate full-year free cash outflow of less than $12 million,” he explained. Corporate and Financial Updates Second quarter 2025 total revenue of $10.3 million, up 7% from the second quarter 2024 Revenue was up year-over-year for each of the past four consecutive quarters Total cash and short-term investments were $24.0 million and total borrowings were $13.2 million at the end of the second quarter 2025 Revenue for the Second Quarter 2025 For the Three Months Ended June 30, For the Six Months Ended June 30, (Dollars in thousands) 2025 2024 2025 2024 Lab Essentials $ 7,792 $ 7,638 $ 15,909 $ 14,904 Clinical Solutions 2,060 1,565 3,222 3,283 Other 435 411 951 717 Total revenue $ 10,287 $ 9,614 $ 20,082 $ 18,904 Second Quarter 2025 Financial Results Total revenue for the second quarter 2025 was $10.3 million, up 7% compared to $9.6 million in the second quarter 2024. Lab Essentials revenue was $7.8 million in the second quarter 2025, up 2% compared to $7.6 million in the second quarter 2024. Clinical Solutions revenue was $2.1 million in the second quarter 2025, up 32% compared to $1.6 million in the second quarter 2024. Gross profit for the second quarter 2025 was $4.0 million, compared to $2.8 million in the second quarter 2024. Gross margin for the second quarter 2025 was 38.7%, compared to 29.2% in the second quarter 2024. The increase in gross margin was driven by manufacturing efficiency gains and higher revenue. Operating expenses for the second quarter 2025 were $7.4 million, compared to $7.9 million in the second quarter 2024. Excluding a non-recurring charge of $0.1 million recorded in the second quarter of 2024 related to a loss contingency, operating expenses were down $0.5 million. The decrease was driven by reduced spending, primarily on insurance and facility costs. Net loss for the second quarter 2025 was $3.6 million, or negative $0.07 per diluted share, compared to $5.4 million, or negative $0.13 per diluted share, for the second quarter 2024. Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter 2025 was negative $0.8 million, compared to negative $2.6 million for the second quarter 2024. Free Cash Flow was negative $2.3 million for the second quarter 2025, compared to negative $3.0 million for the second quarter 2024. A full reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures is included at the end of this release. Reiterates 2025 Outlook Teknova reiterates its fiscal 2025 outlook for revenue and free cash outflow. The Company continues to anticipate total revenue of $39 million to $42 million for the fiscal year ending December 31, 2025. The Company also anticipates free cash outflow of less than $12 million for 2025. Conference Call and Webcast Teknova will host a webcast and conference call on Thursday, August 7, 2025, beginning at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. To access the live webcast, listeners can log onto the call from the Investor Relations section of the Teknova website or by using this link . If you would like to participate in the call, please register for the webcast here to receive a unique PIN number and dial-in information. The webcast will be available for replay on the Company’s website approximately two hours after the event. About Teknova Teknova makes solutions possible. Since 1996, Teknova has been innovating the manufacture of critical reagents for the life sciences industry to accelerate the discovery and development of novel breakthroughs that will help people live longer, healthier lives. We offer fully customizable solutions for every stage of the workflow, supporting industry leaders in molecular diagnostics, synthetic biology, and emerging therapeutic modalities. Our fast turnaround of high-quality agar plates, microbial culture and cryopreservation media, buffers and reagents, and water helps our customers scale seamlessly from RUO to GMP. Headquartered in Hollister, California, with over 180,000 square feet of state-of-the-art facilities, Teknova’s modular manufacturing platform was designed by our team of scientists, engineers, and quality control experts to efficiently produce the foundational ingredients for the discovery and commercialization of next-generation therapies. Non-GAAP Financial Measures This press release contains financial measures that have not been calculated in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). Teknova uses the following non-GAAP financial measures in assessing the performance of its business and the effectiveness of its business strategies: (a) Adjusted EBITDA and (b) Free Cash Flow. Teknova defines Adjusted EBITDA as net loss adjusted for interest income (expense), net, provision for (benefit from) income taxes, depreciation expense, amortization of intangible assets, and stock-based compensation expense. Adjusted EBITDA reflects further adjustments to eliminate the impact of certain items, including certain non-cash and other items that Teknova does not consider representative of its ongoing operating performance. Teknova continues to define Free Cash Flow as cash used in operating activities plus purchases of property, plant, and equipment. Teknova provides Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow in this press release because Teknova believes that analysts, investors, and other interested parties frequently use these measures to evaluate companies in Teknova’s industry and that such measures facilitate comparisons on a consistent basis across reporting periods. Teknova also believes such measures are helpful in highlighting trends in Teknova’s operating results because they exclude items that are not indicative of Teknova’s core operating performance. Investors should consider non-GAAP financial measures in addition to, and not as a substitute for, or as superior to, measures of financial performance prepared in accordance with GAAP. The non-GAAP financial measures presented by Teknova may be different from the non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies. A full reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures is included at the end of this release. Forward-Looking Statements Statements in this press release about future expectations, plans, and prospects, as well as any other statements regarding matters that are not historical facts, may constitute “forward-looking statements.” These statements include, but are not limited to, statements relating to Teknova’s anticipated total revenue, including expectations for 2025 revenue and free cash outflow guidance, and other statements about Teknova’s business prospects, including about Teknova’s profitability, strategy of managing operating expenses, and long-term growth strategy. These forward-looking statements are based on management’s current expectations and beliefs and are subject to risks and uncertainties, all of which are difficult to predict and many of which are beyond Teknova’s control and could cause actual results to differ materially and adversely from those described in the forward-looking statements. These risks and uncertainties include, but are not limited to, demand for Teknova’s products (including the potential delay to or pausing of customer orders); Teknova’s assessment of fundamental indicators of future demand across its target customer base; Teknova’s cash flows and revenue growth rate; Teknova’s supply chain, sourcing, manufacturing, and warehousing; inventory management; risks related to global economic and marketplace uncertainties, including those related to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East; reliance on a limited number of customers for a high percentage of Teknova’s revenue; potential acquisitions and integration of other companies; and other factors discussed in the “Risk Factors” section of Teknova’s most recent periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), including in Teknova’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2024, and subsequent Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q filed with the SEC, all of which you may obtain for free on the SEC’s website at www.sec.gov. title: Building Trust vs. Overcoming Objections: What Sales Reps Need to Know
summary: 14M+ verified local businesses, AI-handwritten outreach that learns from every campaign, and a built-in email delivery system. All in one tool.
body_text: ← Back to the blog Sales Tips Building Trust vs. Overcoming Objections: What Sales Reps Need to Know Griffin Morris · August 25, 2025 Selling to small and local businesses comes down to two critical skills: building trust and overcoming objections. One is proactive, the other reactive. But both are essential if you want to close more deals and keep customers coming back. Building trust is a proactive effort that starts from the very first interaction. It’s about creating honest, value-driven relationships and positioning yourself as a helpful advisor. Overcoming objections , on the other hand, is reactive. It happens when specific concerns arise (about price, timing, or fit) and you need to address them to keep the deal moving forward. Trust lays the foundation. Objection-handling clears the path. Together, they drive short-term wins and long-term relationships. Outline: Why Trust-Building Comes First in Selling to Local Businesses Understanding and Handling Sales Objections How Trust-Building and Objection Handling Work Together Conclusion FAQs Why Trust-Building Comes First in Selling to Local Businesses Local business owners don’t just buy a product; they buy into the person selling it. Trust is your competitive edge. To build that trust , start by personalizing every interaction. Use the business’s name, mention something about their location . It shows you’ve done your homework. Next, practice active listening. Ask thoughtful questions and let them share their challenges. This isn’t the time for a one-size-fits-all pitch. Be transparent about what your product can and can’t do . Honesty goes a long way in building credibility. And most importantly, show up consistently. Follow up with value, not pressure. Send helpful resources, ideas, or insights without expecting anything in return. That’s how you position yourself as a trusted partner, not just another salesperson. “ Establishing trust is better than any sales technique .” — Mike Puglia , Chief Marketing Officer, Kaseya Understanding and Handling Sales Objections Objections are not rejections. They’re clues. They tell you what the business owner is worried about, what they value, and what’s holding them back from saying “yes.” The objections usually fall into a few categories: price, timing, satisfaction with the status quo, authority, and product fit. Here’s how to put the LAER framework (Listen, Acknowledge, Explore, Respond) approach into action for each objection. 1. Price , “It’s too expensive.” Listen: Don’t rush to defend your pricing. Let them explain what feels out of reach. Acknowledge: “ Totally understand, budgets are tight for a lot of businesses right now.” Explore: “Can I ask what you are comparing it to, or what kind of return would make this feel worth it?” Respond: “One of our customers in a similar industry felt the same way, but after two campaigns, they were booking meetings weekly. If we can drive that kind of result, would it feel more aligned with your budget?” 2. Timing, “We don’t have the budget right now.” Listen: Stay quiet and let them share more about their current financial situation. Acknowledge: “Makes sense. A lot of businesses hit a slow season mid-year.” Explore: “When do you usually plan your marketing budget, or is this something that might be revisited next quarter?” Respond: “If timing’s the only blocker, how about we pencil in a follow-up for [month], and I’ll send over a checklist you can use when you’re ready?” 3. Status quo, “I’m happy with what I’ve got” Listen: Let them explain what’s working well for them. Acknowledge: “ That’s great.” Explore: “Is there anything you’d improve or something your current setup can’t quite do?” Respond: “Sometimes we’re not replacing what you use, we’re adding a layer that saves time or gets you more visibility. If I showed you how one business did both, would you be open to taking a quick look?” 4. Authority, “I need to check with my partner.” Listen: Don’t try to push past the gate. Acknowledge: “Of course, this sounds like something worth aligning on.” Explore: “What kind of questions do they usually ask, or is there anything specific I can help you prepare for that conversation?” Respond: “If it’s helpful, I can send over a quick summary you can forward. Or we can loop them into a short call, whatever makes it easier on your end.” By addressing objections thoughtfully, you show that you understand their challenges and can offer solutions tailored to their goals. How Trust-Building and Objection Handling Work Together Trust-building is ongoing and proactive. It starts from day one and continues throughout the relationship. Objection-handling is responsive. It happens when friction appears, and how you handle it can make or break the deal. So when you hear an objection, don’t panic. Lean into it. Use it to uncover what’s really important to them and show that you care. What Happens When You Master Both? When you combine proactive trust-building with thoughtful objection-handling, you create a sales process that’s: Less pushy and more human. Focused on solving real problems. Built on collaboration, not confrontation. You’re not just selling a product—you’re becoming a trusted partner. That leads to higher conversion rates, more loyal customers, and more referrals . Conclusion Building trust helps you open doors and keep relationships strong. Handling objections helps you overcome friction and close more deals. Sales success comes from striking the right balance between these two. Lead with empathy, show you’re invested in their success, and you’ll stand out from every other salesperson in their inbox. FAQs How does trust reduce objections? When prospects believe you understand their business and have their best interest in mind, they’re less likely to question your offer. Trust makes your message easier to believe, and objections easier to overcome. What’s the best way to handle a price objection? Start by exploring what they’re comparing your price to. Share a real case study or explain the long-term value. Budget objections often mask other concerns, so dig deeper before responding. How do you balance trust-building and objection-handling in a short sales cycle? Start with quick wins that build credibility, like relevant insights or local references. When objections come up, stay calm, listen closely, and show that you’re genuinely here to help. title: Pay Per Lead: A Smarter, Performance-Based Approach to Lead Generation
summary: Traditional models like cost-per-click (CPC) or cost-per-impression (CPM) charge for traffic or visibility, not outcomes. body_text: Digital ad spend continues to rise, but conversions often don’t keep pace. Traditional models like cost-per-click (CPC) or cost-per-impression (CPM) charge for traffic or visibility, not outcomes. That’s why more marketers are turning to Pay Per Lead (PPL), a performance-driven model that charges only when a qualified lead is delivered. In this guide, we’ll break down how PPL works, how it compares to other pricing models, and how to maximize ROI with the right strategy. What Is Pay Per Lead? Pay Per Lead is a pricing model where advertisers pay a flat fee for each qualified lead generated by a vendor or partner. Unlike CPC or CPM models, which focus on driving traffic or brand visibility, PPL is rooted in real outcomes: someone submits a form, books a demo, or places a call. The lead type can vary depending on your business. For a SaaS company, it might be a product demo request. For a law firm, it could be an inbound phone call. What matters most is that the lead meets a set of predefined criteria — such as location, job title, or firm size — agreed upon by both parties. How Does Pay Per Lead Work? A typical PPL campaign begins with clear definitions. The advertiser and lead provider establish exactly what is the target audience and the cost of a qualified lead. These agreements often include filters like geography, industry, or job role to ensure leads are relevant. Lead generation can come from many sources: paid search campaigns, social media ads, affiliate sites, or organic channels like content marketing. Once a lead is captured, it’s validated — sometimes through automated tools, sometimes with human review — and delivered via email, CRM integration, or direct API. In successful campaigns, PPL is a win-win: advertisers only pay for real interest, and providers are incentivized to deliver quality. Why Choose Pay Per Lead Over CPC or CPA? Let’s compare: CPC (Cost-Per-Click): You pay each time someone clicks your ad, regardless of whether they take further action. While CPC can drive traffic, it often results in wasted spend if landing pages or targeting are off. CPM (Cost-Per-Mille): You pay per 1,000 impressions. Great for brand awareness, but it’s disconnected from measurable intent. PPL offers a middle ground. You capture prospects at a critical stage—when they’ve expressed interest but haven’t yet converted—giving you a larger pool to nurture. Key Advantages of Pay Per Lead One of the biggest benefits of PPL is predictability. Since you know the cost per lead upfront, it's easier to forecast spend and ROI. This makes budgeting simpler and reduces the financial risk of underperforming campaigns. Another strength lies in lead quality. Because the campaign is tied to predefined criteria, you're not just getting random names, you're receiving contacts that meet your customer profile. PPL also minimizes waste. With proper validation in place, fake or low-quality leads are filtered out, and you're not paying for empty clicks or irrelevant traffic. Lastly, it's scalable. With a stable cost-per-lead, you can increase spend without sacrificing efficiency — a huge advantage for growth-stage companies. What Makes a PPL Campaign Successful? The most important factor is defining your target audience. That starts with understanding your ideal client profile (ICP): Job title, industry, geography, and company size. Messaging is the next consideration. Communicate your offering clearly to avoid any misunderstanding or confusion with leads. Develop a strong call-to-action that will capture leads with the intent you desire. Measurement matters too. Track not just the cost per lead, but how many of those leads become marketing qualified (MQLs), then sales qualified (SQLs), then customers. That’s where the real ROI is found. Common Metrics to Monitor To optimize PPL campaigns, marketers should track: Cost Per Lead (CPL): The amount spent divided by the number of leads generated. A key efficiency benchmark. Lead-to-MQL/SQL Rates: How well leads advance through the funnel. A low CPL is meaningless if leads never convert. Channel-Specific Performance: Understand which platforms drive the best quality at the best price. Revenue Attribution: Tying leads back to actual revenue helps determine lifetime value and return on investment (ROI). Where Kular AI Comes In Kular brings a modern twist to PPL by using AI to automate lead generation. Instead of relying solely on manual workflows, Kular uses AI to: Identify your ideal client profile. Automate outreach across multiple channels. Charge only for leads who positively respond — not just click or fill a form. By combining performance-based pricing with advanced automation, Kular delivers higher-quality leads at scale with less manual effort. It’s ideal for B2B teams looking to scale outreach without increasing headcount or juggling multiple tools. Final Thoughts In an environment where attention is expensive and conversions are unpredictable, Pay Per Lead offers a smarter path forward. You only pay when someone expresses real interest—and that makes every dollar go further. Whether you partner with an agency or use platforms like Kular to take control of your lead funnel, PPL is a powerful model for growth-focused teams. Curious how it could work for you?
